  Every winter except this one, because this year there was Wren.

  Wren was a young vixen, copper-red and thin, born in a spring of floods. She had not yet learned
  what the older foxes knew: that winter was something to survive and nothing more. When the first
  snow fell, she didn't curl into her den. She went out walking.

  She walked the path to the stream and memorized it by the shape of the drifts. She found the
  hollow where the rabbits slept, a soft dip beside a buried log. She noted where the badger's
  tunnel breathed warm air into the cold, melting a small dark circle in the white. Each night she
  walked farther, and each night she remembered more.

  The older foxes laughed at her. "Snow keeps nothing," said Bracken, a grizzled dog-fox with a torn
  ear. "Tomorrow it falls again, and your paths are gone."

  "Then I'll walk them again," said Wren.

  In the deepest part of January, a blizzard came that lasted four days. When it ended, Hollow Wood
  was unrecognizable. Even the trees seemed to have moved. The foxes emerged from their dens, hungry
  and confused, sniffing at a landscape that had become a stranger.

  Bracken stood at the edge of the clearing for a long time. He was old, and his nose wasn't what it
  had been, and he could not find the stream.

  Wren came up beside him, her breath steaming.

  "This way," she said.

  She led him past a drift that hid the fallen oak, around a hummock that covered a sharp stone, and
  down a gentle slope she had walked forty times. There was the stream, black and moving under a
  skin of ice. Bracken drank for a long time.

  When he lifted his head, he looked at her differently.

  "You kept it," he said. "The snow tried to take the wood, and you kept it."

  Wren didn't answer. She was already looking toward the trees, where three other foxes stood
  uncertainly at the clearing's edge.

  She trotted toward them, leaving a line of small, careful footprints behind her. They formed a new
  path across the white.
